noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand how chemists limit the problems caused by polymer disposal by: i developing biodegradable polymers ii removing toxic waste gases produced by the incineration of polymers Further suggested practicals: i investigating the difference in reactivity of alkanes and alkenes, including combustion, reaction with bromine water, reaction with acidified potassium manganate(VII) ii preparation of cyclohexene from cyclohexanol iii preparation of limonene from orange peel by steam distillation iv preparation of Perspex ® from methyl 2-methylpropenoate

primer.text: Plastic survives burial for centuries, so chemists route waste polymers through four different exits. This note weighs landfill against incineration with its toxic flue gases, melt-and-remould recycling, and the biodegradable and compostable polymers engineered to surrender to microbes. Every route has a cost the exam expects you to name.

lessons.title: Landfill and incineration
lessons.opening: The two oldest exits for waste polymer are a hole in the ground and a flame. Landfill consumes land and leaks nothing useful back; incineration recovers heat energy but must scrub the toxic gases its flue carries. Both routes carry costs the exam expects you to weigh.
keyPoints: Landfill disposal consumes land space and stores unreactive polymer for centuries.
Incineration recovers heat energy from burning waste polymers.
Burning halogen-containing polymers such as PVC releases acidic toxic gases, including hydrogen chloride.
Chemists limit the incineration problem by scrubbing toxic waste gases from the flue before release.
Neither route recycles the polymer's material value - one buries it, one burns it.

low.restatement: Bury the plastic and it outlives the landfill; burn it and you get energy but must clean hydrogen chloride and other acidic gases from the smoke first.
low.analogy: Landfill is a freezer that keeps the problem intact; incineration is a furnace that turns the problem into energy plus fumes needing a filter.
low.examPointer: Name hydrogen chloride from PVC combustion - a generic 'toxic gases' answer usually drops the specificity mark.

medium.restatement: The incineration trade-off is energy recovery against flue toxicity: chlorinated backbones oxidise to HCl, so scrubbers neutralise the acid gases before the plume leaves the stack.
medium.analogy: Burning chlorine-bearing plastic is like cooking with a smoke alarm guaranteed to fire - the meal (energy) is real, but the ventilation (scrubbing) is mandatory.
medium.examPointer: When a question asks how chemists 'limit the problems', answer with the gas-removal step, not merely the detection of the gases.

check.stem: Which toxic acidic gas is released when PVC is incinerated?

options.text: Hydrogen chloride, from the chlorine in the polymer
options.explanation: The chlorinated backbone burns to HCl.

options.text: Hydrogen fluoride
options.explanation: PVC carries chlorine, not fluorine.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide
options.explanation: That comes from sulfur impurities in fuels, not PVC.

options.text: Nitrogen monoxide
options.explanation: That forms from air's nitrogen at engine temperatures.

check.stem: What is the main benefit that incineration offers over landfill?

options.text: Heat energy is recovered from the burning polymer
options.explanation: The flame's energy can power recovery systems.

options.text: The polymer is recycled into new plastic
options.explanation: Burning destroys the material value.

options.text: No gases are produced
options.explanation: Combustion always produces flue gases needing control.

options.text: The land becomes fertile
options.explanation: Landfill stores waste; it does not fertilise.

check.stem: Why does landfill remain an unsatisfactory primary disposal route?

options.text: Polymers persist for centuries while consuming land capacity
options.explanation: Unreactive chains barely degrade underground.

options.text: Landfill releases heat energy
options.explanation: Storage releases nothing; burning does.

options.text: Landfill converts polymer to biomass quickly
options.explanation: Ordinary addition polymers resist microbial attack.

options.text: Landfill requires no land
options.explanation: Sites consume large areas.

check.stem: How do chemists limit the problems caused by incinerating halogenated polymers?

options.text: By removing the toxic waste gases from the flue before release
options.explanation: Scrubbing neutralises the acidic products.

options.text: By adding chlorine to the flame
options.explanation: More halogen worsens the acid gas load.

options.text: By burning the polymer at landfill sites
options.explanation: Open burning skips the scrubbing entirely.

options.text: By diluting the polymer with food waste
options.explanation: Dilution does not remove the acidic combustion products.

check.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the two routes?

options.text: Landfill stores the material value; incineration destroys it while recovering energy
options.explanation: Burial preserves (uselessly), burning converts to heat.

options.text: Both routes recover the polymer for reuse
options.explanation: Neither route recycles the material.

options.text: Incineration consumes more land than landfill
options.explanation: Landfill is the land consumer.

options.text: Landfill produces hydrogen chloride
options.explanation: HCl is the incineration problem.

check.stem: State two drawbacks of landfill disposal of polymers.
check.modelAnswer: Landfill consumes land space and the unreactive polymer persists there for centuries without useful recovery.

check.stem: Name the toxic waste gas produced when polymers containing chlorine are burned and state how chemists limit its release.
check.modelAnswer: Hydrogen chloride forms when chlorinated polymers burn; scrubbers remove the toxic waste gases from the flue before they can escape.

check.stem: Explain why incineration is nonetheless still used despite its toxic gas problem.
check.modelAnswer: The heat energy recovered offsets fossil fuel use, and scrubbing technology can capture the acidic gases, so the energy benefit is judged worth the controlled treatment cost.

check.stem: A council must choose between landfill and scrubbed incineration for a PVC waste stream. Give one advantage and one managed disadvantage of the incineration choice.
check.modelAnswer: Advantage: the combustion heat is recovered as useful energy. Managed disadvantage: the PVC releases hydrogen chloride on burning, so the flue must pass through gas scrubbing before any release.

lessons.title: Recycling and biodegradable polymers
lessons.opening: The two constructive routes keep the polymer's value in play. Recycling sorts, melts and remoulds existing chains into new goods; biodegradable polymers invite microbes to dismantle the chain when its useful life ends. Each route solves a different half of the waste problem.
keyPoints: Recycling sorts waste polymers by type, then melts and remoulds them into new products.
Sorting is the costly step, since mixed polymer types ruin each other's properties when melted together.
Biodegradable polymers are engineered so microorganisms can break their chains down.
Biodegradable routes reduce the landfill burden because the polymer is consumed rather than stored.
Both routes preserve material value better than burial or simple burning.

low.restatement: Recycling gives the plastic a second life by melting and remoulding sorted waste; biodegradable plastics are built to be eaten by microbes after use.
low.analogy: Recycling is a wardrobe swap for the polymer; biodegradability is a pre-arranged funeral where the guests (microbes) clean up afterwards.
low.examPointer: Name the sorting difficulty when discussing recycling costs - mixed types contaminate each other when melted.

medium.restatement: The chain architecture decides biodegradability: engineered bonds or starch-derived sections give microbes an attack point, so the polymer fragments biologically instead of persisting like ordinary addition polymer chains.
medium.analogy: Ordinary polymer chains are steel cables to microbes; biodegradable ones are ropes with pre-frayed sections the microbes can unravel.
medium.examPointer: Link biodegradable polymers explicitly to landfill reduction - the specification pairs the two ideas and questions follow that pairing.

check.stem: What is the costly bottleneck of polymer recycling?

options.text: Sorting the waste into separate polymer types
options.explanation: Mixed polymers ruin each other when melted.

options.text: Melting the sorted polymer
options.explanation: Melting is cheap once sorting is done.

options.text: Remoulding the melt
options.explanation: Forming new shapes is routine processing.

options.text: Transporting to landfill
options.explanation: Landfill is the alternative, not a recycling step.

check.stem: How do biodegradable polymers reduce the landfill problem?

options.text: Microorganisms break the polymer chains down after disposal
options.explanation: The material is consumed rather than stored.

options.text: They make landfill sites smaller forever
options.explanation: The benefit is the breakdown, not the site geometry.

options.text: They burn without gases
options.explanation: Burning is a different route entirely.

options.text: They can never be disposed of
options.explanation: Disposal still happens; the polymer then degrades.

check.stem: What happens if different polymer types are melted together during recycling?

options.text: The mixture's properties are ruined for most uses
options.explanation: Incompatible chains weaken the remoulded product.

options.text: The polymers react to form a new useful plastic
options.explanation: No such constructive reaction rescues mixed waste.

options.text: The polymers separate automatically by density
options.explanation: Sorting must be done before melting.

options.text: Nothing happens - all polymers are compatible
options.explanation: Compatibility is exactly what sorting protects.

check.stem: Which property must an engineered polymer possess to be called biodegradable?

options.text: Susceptibility to breakdown by microorganisms
options.explanation: Microbial attack defines the term.

options.text: Solubility in water
options.explanation: Dissolving is not biodegrading.

options.text: A lower melting point than PVC
options.explanation: Melting point is unrelated to biodegradation.

options.text: The ability to burn cleanly
options.explanation: Combustion behaviour is the incineration topic.

check.stem: Which pairing of route and principal benefit is correct?

options.text: Recycling - material value reused; biodegradable - landfill burden reduced
options.explanation: Each route targets a different half of the problem.

options.text: Recycling - energy recovered; biodegradable - material reused
options.explanation: Both benefits are swapped between routes.

options.text: Recycling - no sorting needed; biodegradable - no microbes needed
options.explanation: Both claims are false.

options.text: Recycling - landfill eliminated; biodegradable - energy recovered
options.explanation: Neither benefit belongs to its route.

check.stem: Describe the recycling route for waste polymers in three steps.
check.modelAnswer: Sort the waste by polymer type, melt the sorted polymer, then remould it into new products.

check.stem: State what biodegradable polymers are designed to do and which agents perform it.
check.modelAnswer: They are designed to break down after disposal, with microorganisms attacking and consuming the chains.

check.stem: Explain why recycling preserves more material value than incineration.
check.modelAnswer: Recycling remoulds the existing chains into new goods, keeping the polymer's structure and hence its manufacturing value, whereas burning destroys the chains and returns only their heat content.

check.stem: A drinks company wants its bottles to have a lower landfill impact. State whether biodegradable or ordinary PET suits that goal and why.
check.modelAnswer: A biodegradable polymer suits the goal: after use, microorganisms dismantle its chains, so discarded bottles are consumed instead of persisting in landfill for centuries.

lessons.title: Compostable polymers
lessons.opening: Compostable is a stronger claim than biodegradable: the polymer must not merely fragment but convert, under composting conditions, into carbon dioxide, water and biomass - the same outputs nature returns from a fallen leaf.
keyPoints: Compostable polymers must break down completely under composting conditions.
The required end products are carbon dioxide, water and biomass.
Composting conditions supply the warmth, moisture and microbial community the process needs.
Compostable polymers therefore fit organic waste streams rather than ordinary landfill.
The claim is testable: if toxic residues or fragments persist, the polymer is not compostable.

low.restatement: A compostable polymer finishes the job biodegradation starts: in a compost heap it turns entirely into carbon dioxide, water and biomass.
low.analogy: Biodegradable means the rope frays; compostable means it decomposes into soil, steam and breath - nothing left to pick up.
low.examPointer: List all three end products in exam answers - naming only carbon dioxide is the standard half-mark loss.

medium.restatement: The distinction is endpoint-based: biodegradable covers breakdown to any remnants over any timescale, while compostable demands full conversion to the natural cycling products within managed composting conditions.
medium.analogy: Biodegradable is 'eventually falls apart'; compostable is 'becomes garden soil on schedule'.
medium.examPointer: If asked to distinguish the two terms, contrast the endpoints - fragments versus the full CO2 / water / biomass set.

check.stem: Into what must a compostable polymer convert under composting conditions?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water and biomass
options.explanation: The three natural-cycling products are the requirement.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and monomer only
options.explanation: Biomass and water belong in the product set.

options.text: Methane and landfill gas
options.explanation: That is anaerobic landfill chemistry, not composting.

options.text: It must not convert at all
options.explanation: Conversion is the entire point.

check.stem: Which conditions must composting supply for the polymer to break down fully?

options.text: Warmth, moisture and an active microbial community
options.explanation: Managed compost heaps provide all three.

options.text: Freezing temperatures
options.explanation: Cold slows the microbial chemistry.

options.text: Dry storage
options.explanation: Microbes need moisture to work.

options.text: Strong sunlight
options.explanation: Photodegradation is not the composting mechanism.

check.stem: How does compostable differ from biodegradable as a claim?

options.text: Compostable demands full conversion to the natural products; biodegradable covers fragmentation
options.explanation: The endpoint separates the claims.

options.text: Biodegradable is the stronger claim
options.explanation: Compostable's endpoint is stricter.

options.text: They mean exactly the same thing
options.explanation: The endpoint products distinguish them.

options.text: Compostable polymers never break down
options.explanation: Full breakdown is their requirement.

check.stem: A polymer fragments into small plastic particles in soil but leaves persistent residue. Is it compostable?

options.text: No - persistent residue fails the full-conversion requirement
options.explanation: Compostable means nothing but CO2, water and biomass remains.

options.text: Yes - fragmenting proves compostability
options.explanation: Fragmentation alone is merely some biodegradation.

options.text: Yes, if the fragments are small
options.explanation: Size does not rescue persistence.

options.text: The question cannot be answered
options.explanation: The endpoint evidence settles it.

check.stem: Which waste stream best suits compostable polymers after use?

options.text: Organic waste sent for composting
options.explanation: The polymer joins the managed microbial process.

options.text: Ordinary landfill cells
options.explanation: Landfill lacks the managed composting conditions.

options.text: Incinerator feed
options.explanation: Burning defeats the composting design.

options.text: Ocean disposal
options.explanation: No managed conditions and uncontrolled damage.

check.stem: List the three products that define complete compostable breakdown.
State one practical difference between composting and landfill disposal of polymers.
check.modelAnswer: Composting actively manages warmth, moisture and microbes so the polymer converts fully, while landfill merely stores the polymer under unmanaged conditions.

check.stem: Explain why compostable polymers belong in organic waste streams rather than general waste.
check.modelAnswer: Their designed breakdown needs the managed microbial conditions of composting, which organic waste facilities provide and general waste handling does not.

check.stem: A cafeteria sorts waste into compostables, recyclables and landfill. State where a certified compostable cup should go and what it will become.
check.modelAnswer: The cup goes into the compostable stream, where managed composting converts it into carbon dioxide, water and biomass alongside the organic waste.

glossary.definition: Controlled burning of waste polymers to recover heat energy, requiring flue-gas scrubbing for acidic products.
A polymer engineered so microorganisms can break its chains down after disposal.
A polymer that converts completely into carbon dioxide, water and biomass under managed composting conditions.
Removing toxic waste gases from an incineration flue before release.
